title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Overlapping Schwarz methods are among the most successful domain decomposition preconditioners for large-scale finite element simulations. In this work, the Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW), GDSW$^*$, and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces are studied for three-dimensional high-order finite element method (FEM) and virtual element method (VEM) for the Poisson equation and the equations of linear elasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of GDSW-type coarse spaces for polynomial degrees $k\ge 3$ in three dimensions, for either discretization. In 3D VEM, the face degrees of freedom (DOFs) are moments instead of point values. The kernel of the differential operator, which defines the interface values of the GDSW coarse basis functions, must be represented through these moments. The construction is therefore no longer purely algebraic and, without this correction, the coarse level loses its effect for $k\ge 3$. FEM and VEM are tested on hexahedral meshes, and VEM is additionally tested on polyhedral ones. Polynomial degrees up to $k=5$ and runs on up to $4\,096$ subdomains and parallel cores are included in the numerical study. Numerical experiments show scalable iteration counts for all coarse space variants for the Poisson problem, illustrating the expected trade-off between the coarse space size and robustness. Further experiments for linear elasticity confirms that the moment-based construction extends naturally from the scalar to the vector-valued problem.

infographic.key_insight: GDSW-type coarse spaces enable scalable high-order 3D domain decomposition, but VEM requires moment-based kernel representations to preserve coarse-level effectiveness for polynomial degrees k≥3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These preconditioners support parallel solution of large 3D Poisson and linear-elasticity systems using high-order FEM and VEM.
method: Use two-level overlapping additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW, GDSW*, and RGDSW coarse spaces.
Represent operator kernels through face moments when constructing VEM coarse basis functions.
Evaluate FEM and VEM on hexahedral meshes, with additional polyhedral tests for VEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests reached polynomial degree k=5 and 4,096 subdomains and parallel cores, showing scalable Poisson iteration counts across all coarse-space variants and extension of the moment-based construction to linear elasticity.
infographic.watch_item: VEM coarse-space construction is not purely algebraic: omitting the face-moment correction makes the coarse level ineffective for k≥3.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D

title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
authors: Manish Kumar Singh, Dominic Kang Jueh Lim, Anson Wen Han Cheong, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Chang Quan Lai
abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks identify plate orientations for near-isotropic, ultrastiff closed-cell lattices, with at least six plates required.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a systematic route to lightweight, stiff metamaterials without relying on heuristic design or topology optimization.
method: Use PINNs to solve analytical equations for plate orientations.
Assemble orientations into foam-like geometries and validate with finite element simulations.
Additively manufacture six-plate lattices using LAPIS and characterize experimentally.
infographic.evidence_signal: The lattices reached 90% of the Hashin–Shtrikman stiffness upper bound at relative density 0.4 and a near-isotropic Zener ratio of 0.95 at relative density 0.1.
infographic.watch_item: Suboptimal plate placement introduces bending, limiting how closely realized geometries approach the theoretical stiffness bound.
infographic.paper_title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: Exactly enforcing boundary and initial conditions in a physics-informed neural network enables accurate recovery of the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support nondestructive characterization of shear electromechanical coupling in PMUTs and SAW devices without dedicated destructive resonance tests.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers in network outputs to enforce clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial conditions.
Train on coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse observations, eliminating boundary and initial-condition penalty weights.
Nondimensionalize governing coefficients to comparable scales; use a quadratic temporal multiplier to improve early-time electrostatic consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: In six-way manufactured-data comparisons at 30 dB, constrained variants achieved 0.15–0.51% mean e15 error; the full formulation achieved 1.19% on finite-element data at 30 dB and 0.65–2.71% across 40–0 dB.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based; experimental robustness to model mismatch and imperfectly known boundary conditions remains unverified.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Zhuoli Ouyang, Changxi Chi, Siyuan Li, Tailin Wu
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.

infographic.key_insight: ENGINE combines low-variance subspace updates with high-dimensional corrections to improve memory-efficient zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It transfers variational multiscale ideas from computational mechanics to LLM optimization, treating parameter spaces as coupled coarse and fine scales.
method: Adapt static Variational MultiScale theory to dynamic optimization.
Use a multigrid-style V-cycle to alternate between coarse and fine parameter spaces.
Inject fine-scale information into coarse sampling to reduce variance and correct curvature-induced bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard LLM benchmarks, ENGINE reports higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing zeroth-order methods, with up to 2.61× speed-up in forward passes and no additional peak memory overhead.
infographic.watch_item: Theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions, and the abstract does not specify benchmark coverage or wall-clock speed-ups.
infographic.paper_title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
authors: Tom Saliencro, Wen-Hsuan Liu, Rohan Desai, Amara Okonkwo, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

infographic.key_insight: BISECT counters spectral starvation in continual LoRA learning by dividing a fixed low-rank budget between shared invariant features and task-specific novelty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach may support sequential updates to engineering vision models without inference overhead, but the abstract does not evaluate solid mechanics or constitutive modeling.
method: Build an invariant carrier from dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix.
Extract an orthogonal novelty complement using generalized Rayleigh whitening and complement projection.
Merge trained updates into the frozen backbone, gating invariant atoms by current-to-joint Rayleigh ratios and preserving novelty atoms at unit gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that historical null tails capture only 5.5% of incoming-task variance and that BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines across eight incremental settings on five vision datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Whitening stability and training-time spectral decomposition costs require assessment; zero added inference cost does not imply zero training overhead.
infographic.paper_title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
authors: Wen-Hsuan Liu, Amara Okonkwo, Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

infographic.key_insight: RASP separates reading from learning: inference uses every LoRA atom, while training updates only a sparse subset within one fixed-size adapter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support memory-constrained continual adaptation of engineering vision models, but constitutive modeling and solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated in the abstract.
method: Use a scene-modulated cosine router to select the top-q unlocked atoms for gradient updates while retaining all atoms during inference.
Penalize Gram coherence between updated and non-updated output directions to reduce interference.
Combine activation history and atom spectral norms into a consolidation index that controls step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports matching or surpassing branch-expanding LoRA learners on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A with a constant adapter parameter footprint.
infographic.watch_item: Long-horizon adaptation as atoms become locked remains a concern; the abstract provides no quantitative results or task-horizon details.
infographic.paper_title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA

title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling
authors: Zhihao Niu, Peng Chen, Shenggen Zheng, Yuan-Yuan Zhao, Yuanyuan Zhao
abstract: Coupler geometry controls both the frequency splitting and the dissipation of coupled polygon resonators. We develop a continuum model for two identical square-shaped resonators coupled by a shared tether and compare the analytical predictions with finite element simulations. The model relates the coupler length and width to the frequency splitting and dissipation dilution of the two coupled modes. In the short-coupler limit, $k_cl_c\ll1$, the symmetric-mode coupler undergoes nearly uniform rotation, and its torsional strain energy vanishes asymptotically. The remaining loss contributions arise from polygon-side bending and supporting-tether torsion. The reduced supporting-tether contribution allows the symmetric-mode dissipation dilution to exceed that of an isolated polygon with the same side and supporting-tether dimensions. The antisymmetric mode retains torsional strain in the coupler and has an additional loss contribution. We also derive an expression for $Q\cdot f$ in the short-coupler and short-tether limits, where $Q$ is the mechanical quality factor and $f$ is the resonance frequency. This expression gives the dependence of $Q\cdot f$ on tensile stress, film thickness, and supporting-tether geometry. For a coupler length of $100~μ\mathrm{m}$ and width of $2~μ\mathrm{m}$, finite element calculations give a frequency splitting of $17.7~\mathrm{Hz}$ and a symmetric-mode dilution factor approximately $13\%$ above the analytical isolated-polygon value.

infographic.key_insight: A short shared coupler suppresses symmetric-mode torsional loss, enabling coupled square resonators to exceed the dissipation dilution of an isolated polygon.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupler geometry provides a design lever for tuning frequency splitting and mechanical loss in coupled resonators.
method: Develop a continuum model of two identical square resonators joined by a shared tether.
Relate coupler length and width to mode splitting and dissipation dilution, and compare with finite element simulations.
Derive Q·f scaling in the short-coupler and short-supporting-tether limits.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a 100 μm-long, 2 μm-wide coupler, finite element calculations predict 17.7 Hz frequency splitting and symmetric-mode dilution approximately 13% above the analytical isolated-polygon value.
infographic.watch_item: The reported validation is numerical, and the asymptotic loss suppression and Q·f expression require short-coupler or short-tether conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Coupled Soft-Clamped Polygon Resonators with Tunable Mechanical Coupling

title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method
authors: Run Du, Xuan Xiao, Wenming Cheng, Zeqiang Zhang
abstract: This paper presents a residual-constrained topology optimization framework that controls interface transition bandwidth without requiring external density filters. The steady conserved Allen--Cahn (AC) equation is formulated as an equality residual constraint and solved via a mass-weighted Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM) coupled with the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA). A closed-form chemical potential projection eliminates the constant residual mode, ensuring algebraic compatibility with external volume targets. Variational sensitivity analysis reveals a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian that yields matrix-free sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves, reducing residual sensitivity overhead to only 0.11% of the state elasticity solve time in 3D. Systematic 2D benchmarks confirm that interface bandwidth is governed intrinsically by reaction--diffusion parameters across mesh refinements. While diffuse interfaces incur a continuous compliance elevation (1.4%--12.3%), a volume-preserving 0/1 post-processing audit across 48 benchmark cases demonstrates that this gap stems primarily from intermediate-density penalization: binarized AC-ALM designs achieve equal or superior stiffness in 45 configurations (averaging 1.2% stiffer than SIMP). Simultaneously, single-node hinges and strut fragmentation are substantially suppressed compared to unregularized baselines. Three-dimensional benchmarks further demonstrate practical spatial viability for complex structures.

infographic.key_insight: Constraining the conserved Allen–Cahn residual controls topology interface bandwidth intrinsically, without external density filters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework suppresses single-node hinges and strut fragmentation while supporting complex 3D structural topology optimization.
method: Enforce the steady conserved Allen–Cahn equation using a mass-weighted augmented Lagrangian method coupled with MMA.
Project the chemical potential to eliminate the constant residual mode and maintain compatibility with prescribed volume targets.
Exploit a symmetric-plus-rank-one Jacobian for matrix-free residual sensitivities without additional adjoint PDE solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 48 benchmark cases, volume-preserving binarized designs matched or exceeded SIMP stiffness in 45 cases and averaged 1.2% stiffer; 3D residual sensitivity overhead was 0.11% of elasticity solve time.
infographic.watch_item: Diffuse designs showed 1.4%–12.3% higher compliance, so the reported stiffness advantage applies to volume-preserving binarized designs rather than the continuous optimization outputs.
infographic.paper_title: Allen--Cahn Residual-Constrained Topology Optimization via an Augmented Lagrangian Method

title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
authors: James Malcolm, Clare McColgan, Emma Mullarkey, Emad Chaparian
abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

infographic.key_insight: A 24-arm fractal vane produces nearly axisymmetric yielding, while simulation-informed conversion expressions improve rheological interpretation beyond the circular Couette analogy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain-rate conversions support more accurate material characterization in vane-in-cup rheometers.
method: Model viscoplastic fluids using the Herschel–Bulkley constitutive law.
Use augmented Lagrangian finite elements in 2D and regularised finite volumes in 3D.
Compare 4-arm, 6-arm and 24-arm fractal vanes to assess yielding and refine conversion closures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive 2D and 3D simulations across a broad parameter range, but provides no quantitative accuracy metrics or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: This is a computational rheometry study, not an AI surrogate model; closure applicability beyond the simulated configurations requires verification.
infographic.paper_title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures

title: High-Order Unconditionally Stable IMEX BDF--FEM Schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley Model on a Branched Axon
authors: Hayden Reed, Qingguang Guan
abstract: We construct and analyze high-order implicit--explicit backward differentiation formula finite element (IMEX BDF--FEM) schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley cable system on a branched metric graph. The linearly implicit schemes combine constant-step BDF methods of orders $q=1,\ldots,5$ with conforming finite elements of any fixed degree $p\ge1$. Extrapolated gate variables are smoothly masked before evaluating the conductances, preserving coercivity without projecting the numerical gates. A voltage cutoff makes the gate rates globally bounded and Lipschitz. Each timestep requires one linear voltage solve followed by independent nodal gate updates. Under exact spatial integration, we prove unconditional stability of the complete fully discrete regularized scheme in discrete history energies. Under regularity and starting-history assumptions, the voltage and reconstructed gates converge in $L^2(Γ)$ at the optimal rate $O(h^{p+1}+Δt^q)$, without a timestep restriction or an $h$--$Δt$ coupling. The same rate holds with numerical quadrature when its full residual defect is $O(h^{p+1})$. Manufactured solutions recover the predicted orders through BDF5--$P_4$. Action-potential simulations illustrate pulse propagation and splitting, while a controlled work--precision comparison within the proposed family shows that higher-order variants can reach a prescribed accuracy at much lower runtime along the tested joint-refinement paths.

infographic.key_insight: High-order IMEX BDF–FEM schemes achieve unconditional stability and optimal convergence for a regularized Hodgkin–Huxley model on branched axons, without timestep–mesh coupling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient simulation of electrical pulse propagation and splitting in branched neural cables, with higher-order variants reducing runtime at tested accuracy targets.
method: Combine BDF orders 1–5 with conforming finite elements of any fixed degree p ≥ 1.
Smoothly mask extrapolated gates and apply a voltage cutoff to control conductances and gate rates.
Use one linear voltage solve per timestep, followed by independent nodal gate updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured solutions recover predicted orders through BDF5–P4; action-potential simulations demonstrate propagation and splitting, and within-family work–precision tests show higher-order runtime gains.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern the regularized model and require appropriate solution regularity and starting histories; numerical quadrature must meet the stated residual-defect condition to retain optimal convergence.
infographic.paper_title: High-Order Unconditionally Stable IMEX BDF--FEM Schemes for the Hodgkin--Huxley Model on a Branched Axon

title: A Legendre-Based Modified Extreme Learning Machine for Convection-Diffusion Equations: Steady-State, Continuous-Time, and Discrete-Time Formulations
authors: Gadade Navnath Ankush, Ram Shiromani, Tomas Gandara, Ramon Codina, Sivaram Ambikasaran
abstract: Convection-diffusion equations are fundamental models for transport phenomena, but their numerical solution becomes challenging in convection-dominated regimes due to steep gradients and sharp boundary layers. This motivates the development of accurate approaches capable of effectively resolving such features while avoiding costly iterative optimization. In this study, a modified ELM framework based on shifted Legendre polynomials is developed for convection-diffusion equations in steady-state, continuous-time, and discrete-time formulations. The proposed approach is evaluated on steady and unsteady benchmark problems with relatively high Peclet numbers, including continuous and discontinuous boundary conditions. Finite element method solutions are used as independent solution references. By exploiting the linearity of the governing equations, MELM determines the output weights through a single least-squares solve, avoiding the iterative gradient-based training required by PINNs. The shifted Legendre polynomial basis provides an effective spectral representation for resolving steep gradients and sharp boundary layers. For the DT-MELM formulation, the coefficient matrix remains unchanged across successive time levels, allowing its LU or QR factorization to be computed once and reused. A systematic comparison with PINNs that incorporate advanced training strategies demonstrates that MELM provides higher accuracy and shorter solution times for steady-state and DT-MELM formulations across the benchmark problems considered. In contrast, CT-MELM exhibits scalability limitations as the size of the space--time basis increases. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of MELM for steady-state and discrete-time convection--diffusion problems, while also showing that PINNs provide better scalability for large space--time formulations where global CT-MELM becomes computationally demanding.

infographic.key_insight: Legendre-based modified extreme learning machines deliver higher accuracy and shorter solution times than tested PINNs for steady-state and discrete-time convection–diffusion benchmarks without iterative gradient-based training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers efficient simulation of convection-dominated transport with steep gradients and sharp boundary layers.
method: Represent solutions using shifted Legendre polynomial bases.
Determine output weights through a single linear least-squares solve.
Reuse the coefficient-matrix LU or QR factorization across discrete time steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers steady and unsteady benchmarks at relatively high Peclet numbers, continuous and discontinuous boundary conditions, FEM reference solutions, and PINNs with advanced training strategies.
infographic.watch_item: Global continuous-time MELM becomes computationally demanding as the space–time basis grows; PINNs show better scalability in this setting.
infographic.paper_title: A Legendre-Based Modified Extreme Learning Machine for Convection-Diffusion Equations: Steady-State, Continuous-Time, and Discrete-Time Formulations

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
authors: Eric A. Lass, Carla Joyce C. Nocheseda, Christopher Tandoc, Yong-Jie Hu, Peter K. Liaw
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

infographic.key_insight: The CALPHAD-based Gamma metric modestly improves prediction of tensile ductility in refractory compositionally complex alloys while matching the DFT-based D-parameter in compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gamma could help screen high-temperature structural alloys for room-temperature ductility, a key barrier to practical deployment.
method: Combine the BCC–HCP free-energy difference, BCC (110) surface interfacial free energy, and electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion.
Compare Gamma with established ductility metrics under tension and compression.
Propose combining Gamma with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility to address intrinsic and extrinsic brittleness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stronger correlation with tensile ductility than the D-parameter and comparable performance in compression, but provides no dataset sizes or numerical correlation values.
infographic.watch_item: The tensile improvement is modest, and combining Gamma with oxygen solubility remains a proposed first-order approach rather than demonstrated validation.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys

title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
authors: Meenu Krishnan U., Maryam Hakimzadeh, Indrashish Saha, Meer Mehran Rashid, Lori Graham-Brady, Somdatta Goswami
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

infographic.key_insight: The best surrogate depends on the fracture task: FNO and Latent DeepONet lead on Dataset 1, while diffusion leads on Dataset 2 at a steep inference cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fracture-Bench supports task-specific surrogate selection for uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design by comparing accuracy, speed and model size.
method: Benchmark 1,000 AT2 simulations of a notched-hole plate and 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with stiffness-contrasting inclusions.
Train FNO, DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, UNet and conditional diffusion models on identical splits.
Evaluate a common metric within each dataset alongside training time, inference time and model size.
infographic.evidence_signal: FNO and Latent DeepONet achieve mean test errors of order 10⁻⁶ on Dataset 1; on Dataset 2, diffusion has about one-sixth of UNet's error but takes 706 s per prediction versus 6 ms.
infographic.watch_item: Average errors can obscure near-bifurcation failures: initial cracks less than one grid cell apart can produce qualitatively different paths, and errors concentrate after crack localization.
infographic.paper_title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics

title: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws
authors: Dorian Zeilinger, Felix Engertsberger, Herbert Egger
abstract: High-performance electrical steel used for iron cores of power transformers and generators exhibits complex material behavior. While modeling and simulation of isotropic nonlinear response is well understood, the incorporation of magnetic anisotropy remains challenging. This work proposes to utilize a structured neural network architecture to systematically describe the anisotropic nonlinear anhysteretic magnetic material response of electrical steel sheets. By constructing a convex and smooth co-energy density with dedicated behavior at infinity, we can ensure thermodynamic consistency and correct physical behavior and further guarantee basic mathematical properties which provide well-posedness of corresponding magnetic field problems and efficient numerical solvers. Numerical tests demonstrate the capability of the proposed method to describe strongly anisotropic behavior as well as its robust convergence in finite-element simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A structured neural network models anisotropic, nonlinear anhysteretic magnetism through a smooth, convex co-energy density with controlled behavior at infinity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports physically consistent and numerically robust magnetic-field simulations of electrical steel cores in transformers and generators.
method: Represent magnetic co-energy using a structured neural network.
Enforce convexity, smoothness, and prescribed asymptotic behavior.
Use the resulting constitutive law in finite-element magnetic-field simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests demonstrate strongly anisotropic material responses and robust convergence in finite-element simulations; the abstract gives no quantitative accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation targets anhysteretic response, so hysteresis modeling is outside the stated scope.
infographic.paper_title: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws

title: Rate optimality of AFEM with maximum marking
authors: Yuwen Li
abstract: For Poisson's equation, we prove optimal algebraic convergence rates for adaptive conforming finite element methods driven by standard maximum marking in arbitrary space dimension, for every marking parameter in $(0,1]$. Previously, instance optimality of a modified maximum marking was proved in [L. Diening, C. Kreuzer, and R. Stevenson, Instance optimality of the adaptive maximum strategy, Found. Comput. Math., 16 (2016), pp. 33--68]. The basic ingredients of our anlaysis consists of discrete reliability, discrete efficiency, overlay and closure estimates of local mesh refinement. The discrete efficiency requires a facet-interior node property of simplicial mesh refinement. The novel part of the optimality analysis is an elementary integral-sum argument that converts energy decrease into a cumulative cardinality bound of marked elements, yielding rate optimality without a contraction argument.

infographic.key_insight: Standard maximum marking yields optimal algebraic convergence rates for adaptive conforming FEM applied to Poisson’s equation in arbitrary space dimension, for every marking parameter in (0,1].
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides theoretical support for maximum-based mesh adaptivity in Poisson-type engineering simulations.
method: Combine discrete reliability and efficiency with mesh overlay and closure estimates.
Require a facet-interior node property for discrete efficiency.
Convert energy decrease into cumulative bounds on marked elements using an integral-sum argument, without a contraction argument.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a mathematical rate-optimality proof, not numerical benchmarks or empirical validation.
infographic.watch_item: The theorem concerns Poisson’s equation and requires compatible simplicial refinement; extensions to nonlinear solid mechanics are not established here.
infographic.paper_title: Rate optimality of AFEM with maximum marking

title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
authors: Zhipu Cui, Helin Gong, Shengfeng Zhu
abstract: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model that turns a natural-language problem description into a set of verified optimization results without manual solver-code development or debugging. The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localizes errors using independent sources of evidence, and completes constrained repairs automatically, thereby providing efficient end-to-end automation, autonomous execution, and verifiable results. We evaluated Agent4FreeFem on a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems. Every case passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.

infographic.key_insight: Agent4FreeFem uses an LLM-driven, verification-guided workflow to turn natural-language topology optimization problems into verified results without manual solver-code development or debugging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce expert effort in setting up and executing topology optimization for aerospace, automotive, and mechanical design.
method: Preserve the original problem definition throughout the automated workflow.
Localize errors using independent sources of evidence.
Apply constrained repairs automatically within stage-specific repair budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the reported suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems, every case passed runtime verification and completed within each stage’s repair budget.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify benchmark size or independently establish physical accuracy and optimization quality beyond runtime verification.
infographic.paper_title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization

title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation
authors: Ye Feng
abstract: This paper formulates a kinematically and variationally consistent phase-field theory for cohesive fracture at finite deformation. The theory introduces an independent compliance-damage field, which accommodates both diffuse distributions and singular concentrations. The phase-field is thereby freed from the dual burden of describing crack geometry and material degradation. A rank-one additive split of the deformation gradient makes separation explicit through independent crack-strain and reference-normal fields. All fields are governed by a single principle of minimum potential energy, which consistently couples nonlinear bulk deformation, crack separation, and crack-plane rotation. One-dimensional energy comparisons show that minimization favors Dirac-type concentration of compliance damage and crack strain. Strong displacement discontinuities thus emerge naturally at a finite phase-field length without being prescribed a priori, while the phase-field remains continuous. The concentrated energy recovers the exact bulk--interface structure of a sharp-crack cohesive zone model. General objective hyperelastic bulk potentials and admissible mixed-mode cohesive laws can therefore be prescribed independently, with the nominal traction--separation law unaffected by the bulk law or phase-field length. Diffuse damage can coexist with concentrated cracks, retaining deformation modes for bulk-energy relaxation during nucleation. Two- and three-dimensional examples validate the theory across large stretches, finite rotations, and complex crack paths. Notably, the computed near-tip Cauchy stress closely matches the analytical 1/r crack-tip asymptotic solution of Long et al. (2011) outside the cohesive zone.

infographic.key_insight: Separating compliance damage from the phase field lets sharp cohesive cracks emerge naturally at finite phase-field length while preserving a continuous phase field.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports fracture simulation under large deformation and rotation, with independently prescribed bulk material behavior and mixed-mode traction–separation laws.
method: Introduce independent compliance-damage, crack-strain, and reference-normal fields.
Use a rank-one additive split of the deformation gradient to represent crack separation.
Couple bulk deformation, separation, and crack-plane rotation through minimum potential energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: One-dimensional energy comparisons favor concentrated cracks; 2D and 3D examples test large stretches, rotations, and complex crack paths, with near-tip stress closely matching an analytical 1/r asymptotic solution outside the cohesive zone.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish mesh-convergence requirements or computational cost for resolving concentrated damage and the additional independent fields.
infographic.paper_title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation

title: Scalable Fully Implicit Runge-Kutta Solvers for Time-Dependent Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
authors: Ahsan Ali, Robert C. Kirby
abstract: We consider the efficient numerical solution of time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection governed by the incompressible Boussinesq equations. The coupled velocity-pressure-temperature system presents significant computational challenges arising from incompressibility, buoyancy coupling, convection, and the simultaneous resolution of multiple physical time scales. We present a systematic study of fully implicit Runge-Kutta methods for time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection, together with scalable finite element solvers for the resulting stage-coupled systems. We employ high-order, L-stable Radau IIA methods for temporal integration and investigate Taylor-Hood and Alfeld-Sorokina finite elements in two dimensions, along with Taylor-Hood and enriched macroelement discretizations in three dimensions. The macroelement approaches offer strong local inf-sup stability and patch structures well suited to Vanka-type relaxation. In two dimensions, monolithic multigrid achieves nearly stage-independent outer Krylov iteration counts and maintains robust convergence under mesh refinement. On the same mesh with incremental pressure correction, selected Radau configurations reduce elapsed solve time by 18-32% and yield smaller sampled transient differences relative to a numerical reference solution. Three-dimensional experiments demonstrate favorable parallel scalability with Taylor-Hood elements and substantially improved discrete mass conservation with the enriched macroelement discretization. These results identify regimes in which coupled multistage fully implicit integration is computationally competitive when equipped with appropriate multigrid preconditioners.

infographic.key_insight: Fully implicit Radau IIA time integration can be computationally competitive for Rayleigh–Bénard convection when paired with scalable multigrid preconditioners.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient simulation of buoyancy-driven thermal flows while addressing incompressibility and coupled velocity–pressure–temperature dynamics.
method: High-order, L-stable Radau IIA integration of the incompressible Boussinesq equations.
Taylor–Hood and macroelement finite element discretizations in two and three dimensions.
Multigrid preconditioning of stage-coupled systems, with macroelement patches suited to Vanka relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports nearly stage-independent Krylov iterations and mesh-robust convergence in 2D, 18–32% lower solve times for selected Radau configurations with incremental pressure correction, and favorable parallel scalability with Taylor–Hood elements in 3D.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains depend on the integration configuration, discretization, and preconditioner; the reported speedups should not be assumed universal.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Fully Implicit Runge-Kutta Solvers for Time-Dependent Rayleigh-Bénard Convection

title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
authors: Edoardo Centofanti, Benjamin Pachev, Joshua Steyer, James D. Trotter, Pietro Benedusi
abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

infographic.key_insight: Extending cuDOLFINx to assemble mixed-dimensional interface problems enables end-to-end GPU execution of the cardiac EMI model while preserving high-level FEniCS programming.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The implementation accelerates finite element models with volumetric regions coupled through lower-dimensional interfaces and can support applications beyond cardiac modeling.
method: Add GPU assembly for mixed-dimensional interface coupling in cuDOLFINx.
Combine assembly with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning.
Benchmark CPU and multi-GPU execution on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Strong and weak scaling tests reached 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom; one GH200 node delivered assembly performance comparable to roughly two to three 144-core CPU nodes, depending on scaling regime and geometry.
infographic.watch_item: Solver speedups depend on geometry, preconditioning, and scale; GPU advantages on regular geometries emerged mainly for larger problems and node counts.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling

title: Optimal L^2 Error Estimates for CSLDG Ideal Numerical Solutions in Time-Dependent Compressible Periodic Flows
authors: Zhengrong Xie
abstract: We study the characteristic Galerkin-type semi-Lagrangian discontinuous finite element (CSLDG) method for conservative linear transport equations. When the characteristic maps and upstream regions are exact, each update of the ideal CSLDG scheme is equivalent to exact conservative transport of the current numerical solution followed by L^2 projection onto the background DG space. The conventional estimate obtained by accumulating projection errors over successive time steps loses one order when Δt\asymp h, but this loss does not represent the actual accuracy of the scheme. For smooth velocity fields \A(\x,t) on a common periodic lattice, we construct local correctors used only in the analysis on uniform Cartesian meshes, assuming that Δt/h is fixed and that every component of the local Courant vector remains uniformly separated from the integers throughout the space-time domain. We prove strict contraction of the reference-cell transport-projection operator on the zero-mean polynomial space, establish uniform solvability of the corrector equation and Lipschitz estimates with respect to its parameter, and control the difference between the exact flow map and a local frozen translation through weak integral moments. This yields a one-step residual of order O(h^{K+2}), and, while retaining the step-by-step update and the standard L^2-projected initial data, gives, for the P^K approximation, an optimal O(h^{K+1}) error bound. The velocity may depend on both space and time, and incompressibility is not required. An appendix extends the analysis to a compact-support setting, in which the velocity field and the solution need not share a common spatial period.

infographic.key_insight: Ideal CSLDG achieves optimal O(h^{K+1}) L² accuracy for conservative transport in time-dependent compressible flows, avoiding the apparent order loss in conventional error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result strengthens accuracy guarantees for high-order transport discretizations relevant to computational flow simulations, including compressible velocity fields.
method: Express each ideal update as exact conservative transport followed by L² projection onto the DG space.
Construct analysis-only local correctors using strict contraction of a reference-cell transport-projection operator.
Control flow-map approximation through weak integral moments to obtain an O(h^{K+2}) one-step residual.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical optimal-error proof for P^K approximations with standard L²-projected initial data, not numerical benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The proof assumes exact characteristic maps and upstream regions, uniform Cartesian meshes, fixed Δt/h, and local Courant components uniformly separated from integers.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal L^2 Error Estimates for CSLDG Ideal Numerical Solutions in Time-Dependent Compressible Periodic Flows
